title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: Before the start of the campaign, Rostov had received a letter from his parents in which they told him briefly of Natasha's illness and the breaking off of her engagement to Prince Andrew (which they explained by saying that Natasha had rejected him), and again asked Nicholas to retire from the army and return home. On receiving this letter, Nicholas didn't even try to get leave or to retire, but wrote to his parents that he was sorry Natasha was ill and her engagement broken off, and that he would do all he could to meet their wishes. To Sonya he wrote separately.

"Adored friend of my soul!" he wrote. "Nothing but honor could keep me from returning to the country. But now, at the start of the campaign, I would feel dishonored — not only in my comrades' eyes but in my own — if I preferred my own happiness to my love and duty to the Fatherland. But this shall be our last separation. Believe me, as soon as the war is over, if I am still alive and still loved by you, I will throw up everything and fly to you, to press you forever to my loving heart."

It was in fact only the start of the campaign that prevented Rostov from returning home as he had promised and marrying Sonya. The autumn in Otradnoe with the hunting, and the winter with the Christmas holidays and Sonya's love, had opened up to him a vision of tranquil rural joys and peace such as he had never known before, and which now beckoned to him. "A wonderful wife, children, a good pack of hounds, a dozen leashes of swift borzois, farming, neighbors, elected public service..." he thought. But now the campaign was beginning, and he had to stay with his regiment. And since it had to be so, Nicholas Rostov, as was natural to him, found contentment in the life he led in the regiment and managed to find pleasure in it.

On his return from his leave, Nicholas was joyfully welcomed by his comrades and sent to buy remount horses. He brought back from Ukraine excellent horses that pleased him and earned him praise from his commanders. During his absence he had been promoted to captain, and when the regiment was put on a war footing with increased numbers, he was again given command of his old squadron.

The campaign began, the regiment was moved into Poland on double pay, new officers arrived, new men and horses, and above all everybody was infected with the merrily excited mood that goes with the start of a war. Rostov, conscious of his good standing in the regiment, devoted himself entirely to the pleasures and interests of military service, though he knew that sooner or later he would have to give them up.

The troops retreated from Vilna for various complicated reasons of state, political and strategic. Each step of the retreat was accompanied by a complex interplay of interests, arguments, and passions at headquarters. For the Pavlograd hussars, however, the whole retreat during the finest period of summer, with adequate supplies, was a very simple and pleasant affair.

It was only at headquarters that there was depression, uneasiness, and intrigue; in the body of the army no one asked where they were going or why. If they were sorry to retreat, it was only because they had to leave billets they had grown used to, or some pretty young Polish lady. If the thought that things looked bad happened to enter anyone's head, he tried to be as cheerful as befits a good soldier and not to think about the big picture, but only about the task nearest at hand. First they camped cheerfully near Vilna, making friends with the Polish landowners, preparing for reviews, and being reviewed by the Emperor and other high commanders. Then came an order to retreat to Sventsiany and destroy any supplies they couldn't carry. Sventsiany was remembered by the hussars only as "the drunken camp" — a name the whole army gave to their time there — because many complaints were made against the troops, who, using the order to collect supplies as cover, also took horses, carriages, and carpets from the Polish landowners. Rostov remembered Sventsiany because on the first day of their arrival in that small town he had to replace his sergeant major and was unable to manage all the drunken men of his squadron, who had secretly appropriated five barrels of old beer. From Sventsiany they retreated farther and farther to Drissa, and then beyond Drissa, drawing close to the Russian heartland.
On July thirteenth the Pavlograds took part in a serious engagement for the first time.
On the twelfth of July, the eve of that action, there was a violent storm of rain and hail. In general, the summer of 1812 was remarkable for its storms.

The two Pavlograd squadrons were camped in a field of rye, already in ear but completely trampled by cattle and horses. The rain was falling in torrents, and Rostov with a young officer named Ilyin, his protege, was sitting in a hastily built shelter. An officer of their regiment, with long mustaches extending onto his cheeks, who after riding to the staff had been caught by the rain, came into Rostov's shelter.
"I've come from the staff, Count. Have you heard about Raevsky's exploit?"
And the officer gave them details of the Saltanov battle, which he had heard at the staff.

Rostov, smoking his pipe and turning his head as the water trickled down his neck, listened with half an ear, with an occasional glance at Ilyin, who was pressing close beside him. This officer, a boy of sixteen who had recently joined the regiment, now stood in the same relation to Nicholas that Nicholas had been to Denisov seven years before. Ilyin tried to imitate Rostov in everything and adored him as a girl might have done.

Zdrzhinski, the officer with the long mustaches, spoke grandly of the Saltanov dam being "a Russian Thermopylae" and of how a deed worthy of antiquity had been performed by General Raevsky. He described how Raevsky had led his two sons onto the dam under terrific fire and had charged with them beside him. Rostov heard the story and not only said nothing to encourage Zdrzhinski's enthusiasm but, on the contrary, looked like a man ashamed of what he was hearing, though with no intention of contradicting it. Since the campaigns of Austerlitz and 1807, Rostov knew from experience that men always lie when describing military exploits, as he himself had done when telling them; besides, he had enough experience to know that nothing in war happens the way we can imagine or describe it. And so he didn't like Zdrzhinski's tale, nor did he like Zdrzhinski himself, who with his mustaches extending over his cheeks, leaned low over his listener's face as was his habit, crowding Rostov in the cramped shelter. Rostov looked at him in silence. "In the first place, there must have been such confusion and crowding on the dam being attacked that if Raevsky did lead his sons there, it could only have affected about a dozen men nearest to him," he thought. "The rest couldn't have seen who came onto the dam with Raevsky. And even those who did see wouldn't have been much inspired, because what did they care about Raevsky's tender paternal feelings when their own lives were at stake? And besides, the fate of the Fatherland didn't depend on whether they took the Saltanov dam or not, as we're told was the case at Thermopylae. So why would he have made such a sacrifice? And why bring his own children into battle? I wouldn't have brought my brother Petya there, or even Ilyin, who's a stranger to me but a nice lad — I would have tried to put them somewhere under cover," Nicholas continued to think as he listened to Zdrzhinski. But he didn't express his thoughts, for in such matters too he had learned from experience. He knew that this tale redounded to the glory of the Russian army and so one had to pretend not to doubt it. And he acted accordingly.

"I can't stand this any more," said Ilyin, noticing that Rostov didn't enjoy Zdrzhinski's conversation. "My stockings and shirt... and the water's running into my seat! I'll go look for shelter. The rain seems lighter."
Ilyin went out and Zdrzhinski rode away.
Five minutes later Ilyin, splashing through the mud, came running back to the shelter.
"Hurrah! Rostov, come quick! I've found it! About two hundred yards away there's a tavern where our fellows have already gathered. We can at least get dry there, and Mary Hendrikhovna's there."

Mary Hendrikhovna was the wife of the regimental doctor, a pretty young German woman he had married in Poland. The doctor, whether from lack of means or because he didn't like to be separated from his young wife in the early days of their marriage, took her along with him wherever the hussar regiment went, and his jealousy had become a standing joke among the hussar officers.

Rostov threw his cloak over his shoulders, shouted to Lavrushka to follow with the things, and — now slipping in the mud, now splashing right through it — set off with Ilyin in the lessening rain and the darkness that was occasionally torn by distant lightning.
"Rostov, where are you?"
"Here. What lightning!" they called to one another.
